name: Flint and chert
date_note: used from the Lower Palaeolithic; Neolithic flint mines (Spiennes, Grimes Graves, Krzemionki) c.4000–2000 BCE
making_significance: A fine-grained silica rock that fractures predictably, the main material of knapped tools in many regions.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons; UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out)

name: Obsidian
date_note: obsidian handaxe workshop at Melka Kunture, Ethiopia c.1.2 Ma; widely used thereafter
making_significance: Volcanic glass gives the sharpest stone edges and can be chemically traced to its source, making it a key to mapping networks.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons
notes: Checked: obsidian handaxe workshop at Simbiro III, Melka Kunture, dated >1.2 Ma (Mussi et al. 2023).

name: Nephrite
date_note: Xinglongwa c.6200–5400 BCE; Hetian (Khotan) nephrite; Taiwan Fengtian; Aotearoa pounamu
making_significance: A tough amphibole stone worked by abrasion into ritual and status objects in China, Taiwan and Aotearoa.
leaves_out: Pounamu is a taonga owned by Ngāi Tahu under statute.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data; Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked; otherwise link out)

name: Jadeite
date_note: Itoigawa, Japan (Jōmon) c.5000 BCE; Alpine jadeitite axes (Monte Viso) 5th millennium BCE; Motagua Valley, Guatemala; Myanmar jadeite in China from 18th c.
making_significance: A pyroxene stone used in Olmec and Maya greenstone, Jōmon beads, Neolithic European axes and later Qing carving.
leaves_out: Myanmar jade mining linked to conflict and deadly landslides.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Lapis lazuli
date_note: Badakhshan (Sar-i Sang) lapis in Mesopotamia and Egypt from 4th millennium BCE; Chilean lapis in the Andes
making_significance: A deep blue rock from very few sources, carried long distances for beads, inlay and later ground as ultramarine pigment.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Carnelian
date_note: Gujarat sources (e.g. Ratanpur) worked from Harappan times; ongoing at Khambhat
making_significance: A red chalcedony, heated to deepen its colour, drilled into beads and carved into seals and rings.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Turquoise
date_note: Sinai mines from early dynastic Egypt; Nishapur (Iran); Cerrillos (New Mexico); Hubei; earlier use in Iran
making_significance: A blue-green copper aluminium phosphate carved and inlaid from Egypt and Iran to the American Southwest and Tibet.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Marble
date_note: Cycladic figures c.3000 BCE; Paros, Pentelikon, Carrara, Proconnesus, Makrana
making_significance: Crystalline limestone that takes a fine polish, quarried for sculpture and building from the Cyclades to the Taj Mahal.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; Europeana

name: Soapstone and steatite
date_note: Indus seals c.2600 BCE (much earlier use); Great Zimbabwe birds; Sierra Leone nomoli; Inuit carving commercialised from 1949
making_significance: A soft talc-rich stone easily carved and, as steatite, glazed or fired hard.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Basalt
date_note: used from the Palaeolithic; approximate
making_significance: A hard volcanic rock used for grinding stones, Olmec colossal heads and Polynesian adzes.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Rock crystal
date_note: ancient; Fatimid carving 10th–11th c.
making_significance: Transparent quartz, carved and hollowed with abrasive wheels, made Fatimid ewers, reliquaries and seals.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Alabaster
date_note: Egyptian (Hatnub) calcite from early dynastic period; Nottingham alabaster 14th–16th c.
making_significance: Soft translucent stones carved into vessels, figures and window panes.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Amber
date_note: Baltic amber used from Late Palaeolithic; Burmese and Dominican amber
making_significance: Fossilised tree resin carved into beads and ornaments, traded south along the Amber Road.
leaves_out: Burmese (Kachin) amber mining linked to armed conflict.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; Europeana

name: Red coral
date_note: ancient Mediterranean harvesting; traded to India and Tibet; Benin royal regalia from 16th c.
making_significance: Mediterranean red coral was traded to India, Tibet and West Africa, where Benin court regalia used it heavily.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Emerald
date_note: Egyptian mines (Mons Smaragdus) Roman period; Muisca use of Colombian emeralds; exported to Mughal and Ottoman courts from 16th c.
making_significance: Colombian emeralds, mined under Spanish rule, were carved at Mughal and Ottoman courts.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Garnet
date_note: Sri Lankan and Indian garnets in Merovingian and Anglo-Saxon cloisonné 5th–7th c.
making_significance: Thin-cut garnets set over patterned gold foil made cell-work jewellery such as the Sutton Hoo fittings.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Diamond
date_note: India (Golconda) as sole source into 18th c.; Brazil from 1720s; Kimberley from 1867
making_significance: Diamonds from India, then Brazil and South Africa, were cut into faceted gems; 20th-c. mining tied to conflict and migrant labour.
leaves_out: Enslaved miners in Brazil; South African migrant labour; conflict diamonds.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Mica
date_note: Hopewell cut-outs c.100 BCE–500 CE; Indian mica for 20th-c. electronics and cosmetics
making_significance: Sheet mica was cut into Hopewell hands and figures and later mined for electrical insulation and cosmetics.
leaves_out: Child labour in modern Indian mica mining.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles

name: Earthenware
date_note: earliest vessels c.18 ka (China); figurines c.26 ka
making_significance: Porous low-fired clay, the most widespread ceramic body, used for cooking pots, figures and building tiles.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Stoneware
date_note: Shang proto-stoneware; Rhenish stoneware from 14th c.
making_significance: Clay fired to vitrification, dense and waterproof, suited to storage jars and tea wares.
materials_techniques: high firing; ash and salt glazes
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Kaolin and porcelain stone
date_note: Chinese white wares 6th c.; name from Gaoling near Jingdezhen; Cornish china clay from 1740s
making_significance: White clay and a feldspathic stone combined make porcelain; European potters hunted for sources for centuries.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Faience (quartz-frit body)
date_note: Predynastic Egypt; Harappan
making_significance: A non-clay ceramic of ground quartz and alkali that forms its own glaze.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Native copper
date_note: Anatolia c.8th millennium BCE; Great Lakes Old Copper Complex
making_significance: Naturally pure copper hammered without smelting in Anatolia and around Lake Superior.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Arsenical copper
date_note: 4th millennium BCE; Andes later
making_significance: Copper alloyed with arsenic, usually through ore choice, harder than pure copper.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Tin
date_note: approximate; Cornwall, Erzgebirge, Malay Peninsula, Jos Plateau, Bolivia
making_significance: Tin, rarely found near copper, was traded far to make bronze and later pewter and tinplate.
leaves_out: Chinese labour in Malayan mines; Bolivian miners.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries (US public domain)

name: Bronze
date_note: regular use c.3000 BCE in West Asia; China c.2000 BCE
making_significance: A copper–tin alloy that casts well, used for weapons, vessels, bells, drums and statues.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Brass
date_note: Roman cementation brass c.1st c. BCE; European brass manillas traded to West Africa 15th–19th c.
making_significance: A copper–zinc alloy; European brass manillas were melted by Benin casters for plaques and heads.
leaves_out: Manillas were used in the trade in enslaved people.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Gold
date_note: Varna necropolis c.4500 BCE
making_significance: A soft, non-tarnishing metal hammered, cast and granulated for display and currency.
functions: rule and display;exchange and value;ritual and belief
leaves_out: Mining labour and colonial melting of American goldwork.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Silver
date_note: cupellation from 4th millennium BCE; Laurion; Potosí from 1545; Iwami Ginzan 16th–17th c.
making_significance: Spanish American and Japanese silver became the world's money in the 16th–18th c., drawn to China.
leaves_out: Andean mita labour and enslaved miners; enslaved miners at Laurion.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out)

name: Tumbaga
date_note: first millennium BCE–CE onward
making_significance: A gold–copper alloy of the Isthmus and Colombia, surface-enriched to look gold.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Iron
other_names: wrought iron; cast iron; meteoritic iron
date_note: meteoritic iron beads c.3200 BCE; smelted iron widespread c.1200 BCE
making_significance: The most abundant structural metal, first from meteorites and then smelted in bloomeries and blast furnaces.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Steel
date_note: crucible steel c.3rd c. BCE in South India; mass production from 1856
making_significance: Iron with controlled carbon, hardened by quenching; made in crucibles, by forging and later in converters.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Zinc
date_note: Zawar c.9th c.; Chinese zinc from 16th c.
making_significance: Metallic zinc, hard to smelt because it vaporises, was first made in quantity in Rajasthan.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles

name: Lead
date_note: lead beads at Çatalhöyük c.6500 BCE
making_significance: A soft, heavy metal used in pipes, glazes, lead white and type metal, and a long-running occupational poison.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Platinum
date_note: La Tolita–Tumaco culture c.600 BCE–300 CE; European description 1748
making_significance: La Tolita–Tumaco smiths sintered platinum grains with gold, centuries before Europe could melt the metal.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Aluminium
date_note: isolated 1825; Hall–Héroult process 1886
making_significance: A light metal made cheap by electrolysis from bauxite, used in aircraft, furniture and packaging.
leaves_out: Bauxite mining in Guinea, Jamaica and Australia.
free_sources: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries (US public domain); Wikimedia Commons

name: Mercury
date_note: approximate; Almadén (Spain); Huancavelica (Peru) from 1560s
making_significance: Liquid metal used in fire gilding, silver amalgamation and mirrors, mined at Almadén and Huancavelica at great human cost.
free_sources: UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Glass (soda-lime and plant-ash)
date_note: glass beads in Mesopotamia c.2500 BCE; vessels c.1500 BCE
making_significance: Silica melted with a flux (natron, plant ash or potash) and lime makes glass, one of the earliest synthetic materials.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Ochre
date_note: ochre use c.300 ka; processing kits c.100 ka
making_significance: Iron-oxide earths ground into red and yellow pigment, used for body paint, rock art, burial and hide processing.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles

name: Carbon black
date_note: used since the Palaeolithic
making_significance: Soot and charcoal, the base of rock art, inks and lacquers.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Indigo
date_note: Huaca Prieta, Peru c.6,200 years ago; Indigofera in South Asia; woad in Europe; synthetic from 1897
making_significance: The world's main blue dye, extracted from several plants, grown on plantations in Bengal and South Carolina and displaced by synthetic indigo.
leaves_out: Enslaved indigo growers in South Carolina; Bengal ryots (Indigo revolt 1859–60).
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms); Library of Congress (public-domain items); Wikimedia Commons

name: Madder
date_note: Mohenjo-daro madder-dyed cotton (as usually cited); synthetic alizarin 1869
making_significance: Root of Rubia species gives mordant reds from Indian chintz to Turkey red.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Cochineal
date_note: Andean textiles first millennium BCE; New Spain export from 1520s
making_significance: A scale insect farmed on nopal, giving crimson and carmine that became a major Spanish colonial export.
materials_techniques: insect farming; mordant dyeing; lake pigments
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Tyrian purple
date_note: Minoan Crete c.18th c. BCE; Levantine production
making_significance: Dye from murex snails, costly because thousands of snails were needed for one garment.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles

name: Lac
date_note: long-standing in South and Southeast Asia; shellac for 78 rpm records 1890s–1950s
making_significance: Secretions of the lac insect give a red dye and shellac resin used for varnish, bangles, sealing wax and gramophone records.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Saffron
date_note: Akrotiri 'saffron gatherers' fresco c.1600 BCE
making_significance: Hand-picked crocus stigmas yield a costly yellow dye, pigment and spice.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Maya blue
date_note: Classic Maya; earlier claims from c.300 BCE
making_significance: Indigo bound into palygorskite clay by heating makes a stable blue used on murals, sculpture and sacrificial offerings.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles

name: Ultramarine
date_note: Bamiyan murals c.6th–7th c.; European painting from 14th c.; synthetic 1826–28
making_significance: Blue pigment extracted from lapis lazuli by kneading with wax and lye, costlier than gold in Renaissance Europe.
free_sources: National Gallery of Art Washington Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Vermilion and cinnabar
date_note: cinnabar at Çatalhöyük c.7th millennium BCE; Chinese lacquer and seals; Almadén
making_significance: Mercury sulphide ground or synthesised into a brilliant red for lacquer, seals, murals and tombs.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Orpiment
date_note: ancient; used in Egyptian, Chinese and Persianate painting
making_significance: A toxic arsenic sulphide ground into a bright yellow pigment.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Egyptian blue
date_note: early dynastic Egypt c.3200 BCE; Roman
making_significance: The first known synthetic pigment, made by heating sand, copper, lime and natron.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Lead white
date_note: Greek and Roman; stack process in Netherlands 17th c.
making_significance: Lead corroded by vinegar vapour made the main white paint and cosmetic, poisoning workers and wearers.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Malachite and azurite
date_note: malachite eye paint in Badarian Egypt c.4000 BCE
making_significance: Ground copper minerals gave greens and blues for eye paint, East Asian painting and European panels.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Prussian blue
date_note: Berlin c.1706; imported to Japan from 1820s
making_significance: An early synthetic pigment that reached Japan and coloured Hokusai's Great Wave.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Art Institute of Chicago (CC0 images); Wikimedia Commons

name: Synthetic aniline dyes
date_note: mauveine 1856; alizarin 1869; indigo 1897
making_significance: Coal-tar dyes gave new colours and undercut natural dye economies in India and elsewhere.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Google Patents / national patent offices (public documents)

name: Cotton
date_note: cotton fibres at Mehrgarh c.6th–5th millennium BCE; Andean cotton c.4000 BCE; domesticated independently in the Old and New Worlds
making_significance: A seed fibre domesticated at least twice; Indian cottons then American slave-grown cotton organised much of the world economy.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); Library of Congress (public-domain items); Wikimedia Commons

name: Flax and linen
date_note: dyed wild flax fibres at Dzudzuana c.30 ka (contested); linen at Nahal Hemar c.6500 BCE
making_significance: Bast fibre from flax stems, spun and woven into linen, the main cloth of ancient Egypt and much of Europe.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Wool
date_note: woolly sheep and wool textiles c.4th millennium BCE; approximate
making_significance: Sheep fleece spun and felted into cloth, carpets and tents; medieval English wool drove Flemish and Italian cloth industries.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Silk
date_note: silk fabric at Qianshanyang c.2700 BCE; earlier traces claimed
making_significance: Continuous filament from domesticated silkworms, woven into the damasks and brocades exchanged across Eurasia.
functions: clothing and adornment;rule and display;exchange and value
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data; Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Wild silks
other_names: tussar; eri; muga; landibe; Coan silk
date_note: Harappan wild silk fibres c.2450–2000 BCE (Good et al. 2009); Malagasy landibe; Greek Coan silk
making_significance: Silks from undomesticated moths, spun rather than reeled, used in India, Madagascar and the ancient Aegean.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Hemp
date_note: approximate; China Neolithic; Korean sambe; European rope and sailcloth
making_significance: A strong bast fibre used for cloth, rope, sails and paper.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Ramie
date_note: approximate; Echigo-jōfu and Ojiya-chijimi (UNESCO 2009)
making_significance: A lustrous nettle-family bast fibre woven into fine summer cloth in China, Korea and Japan.
free_sources: ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms); Wikimedia Commons
notes: Earliest date uncertain; ramie is among the bast fibres identified at waterlogged Neolithic sites in southern China (c. 6000–3500 BCE); start kept approximate.

name: Jute
date_note: mechanised Dundee jute industry from 1830s; long used in Bengal
making_significance: A coarse bast fibre from Bengal, mechanically spun in Dundee and Calcutta into sacking for global commodity trade.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Camelid fibre
date_note: approximate; Inca cumbi cloth; ongoing
making_significance: Soft fleece of Andean camelids was woven into cumbi cloth, the most valued Inca goods.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Qiviut
date_note: Oomingmak cooperative from 1969; earlier Indigenous use
making_significance: The fine underwool of muskoxen, gathered and knitted by Alaska Native knitters.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Agave fibre
date_note: early Holocene cordage; Yucatán henequen boom late 19th–early 20th c.
making_significance: Agave leaf fibre made Mesoamerican cloth and cordage; henequen plantations in Yucatán used Maya debt labour.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Raffia
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: Palm-leaf fibre woven on single-heddle looms into Kongo and Kuba cloth, once used as currency.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); British Museum EMKP (CC)

name: Barkcloth fibre
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: Inner bark of paper mulberry and figs, carried across the Pacific by voyagers, beaten into tapa.
free_sources: Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked; otherwise link out); Auckland Museum Online Collection (CC BY where marked)

name: Coir
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: Fibre from coconut husk, plaited into sennit for lashing Pacific canoes and houses and stitching sewn boats.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Pandanus
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: Pandanus leaves are processed into strips and plaited into mats, sails and baskets.
free_sources: Auckland Museum Online Collection (CC BY where marked); Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked; otherwise link out)

name: Abaca
date_note: long-standing; export boom 19th c.
making_significance: Banana-family fibre woven into T'boli t'nalak and exported as Manila rope and paper.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Piña
date_note: approximate; prized in the 18th–19th c.; ongoing in Aklan
making_significance: Fine pineapple-leaf fibre woven into translucent cloth for the barong and embroidered textiles.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Harakeke
date_note: Māori use from settlement; 19th-c. export flax trade
making_significance: Leaves provide muka fibre for cloaks and strips for plaiting; 19th-c. traders exchanged muskets for it.
free_sources: Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked; otherwise link out); Auckland Museum Online Collection (CC BY where marked)

name: Elephant ivory
date_note: long-standing; CITES trade ban 1989
making_significance: Tusks carved into figures, oliphants, combs and piano keys; demand drove killing and forced porterage.
functions: rule and display;play and music;ritual and belief
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Walrus ivory
date_note: Arctic use ancient; Norse Greenland export 11th–14th c.
making_significance: Walrus tusk was carved by Arctic peoples and exported from Norse Greenland to Europe, as in the Lewis chessmen.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Bone
date_note: since the Palaeolithic
making_significance: Bone was split and carved into needles, points, flutes and handles.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Antler
date_note: since the Palaeolithic
making_significance: Shed deer and reindeer antler, softened by soaking, was made into points, combs and spear-throwers.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Horn
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: Horn keratin can be heated, flattened and moulded into cups, spoons, lantern panes and bow laminates.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Tortoiseshell
date_note: long-standing; CITES 1977
making_significance: Hawksbill turtle shell, heat-welded into combs, boxes and inlay, drove turtle hunting from the Caribbean to the Pacific.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Spondylus
date_note: Aegean Neolithic c.5500 BCE; Andes c.2500 BCE onward
making_significance: Red and orange Spondylus shell was a valuable carried inland in Neolithic Europe and the Andes.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Cowrie
date_note: Shang China c.1200 BCE; Maldivian exports into 19th c.
making_significance: Small Indian Ocean shells used as money and ornament from China to West Africa.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); British Museum EMKP (CC)

name: Conch shell
date_note: Harappan shell bangles; ongoing in Bengal
making_significance: Sacred chank shell from the Gulf of Mannar was sawn into bangles and made into trumpets.
functions: ritual and belief;clothing and adornment;play and music
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Pearl and mother-of-pearl
date_note: Gulf pearling ancient to 1930s; Caribbean pearl fisheries with enslaved divers 16th c.
making_significance: Pearls and shell nacre were set, inlaid and carved; pearl diving in the Gulf and Caribbean was dangerous forced or bonded work.
leaves_out: Enslaved Indigenous and African divers; debt-bonded Gulf divers.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1 where marked); Qatar Digital Library (licence per item; check)

name: Feathers
date_note: long-standing; 19th-c. plume trade
making_significance: Feathers were knotted into cloaks and mosaics; 19th-c. fashion plume hunting prompted bird-protection law.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked; otherwise link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Leather
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: Tanned animal skin used for footwear, containers, armour and bookbinding.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Rawhide
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: Untanned hide dries rigid and was used for cases, drums, shields and lashing.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Fish skin
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: Salmon and carp skin prepared as supple leather for clothing and bags in Amur, Ainu and Alaskan communities.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Sinew
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: Dried tendon split into thread for sewing and used as backing on composite bows.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Beeswax
date_note: beeswax residues on Anatolian pots c.7th millennium BCE
making_significance: Wax for lost-wax casting, batik resist, encaustic, candles and sealing.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Ostrich eggshell
date_note: engraved water containers at Diepkloof c.60 ka; beads c.50 ka
making_significance: Ostrich eggshell was engraved as water flasks and ground into beads in southern and eastern Africa.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles

name: Baleen and whale bone
date_note: Arctic use ancient; commercial whaling 17th–20th c.
making_significance: Baleen's springy plates were used by Arctic peoples for baskets and by industrial whalers' customers for corsets.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Dentalium shell
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: Tusk shells from Vancouver Island waters circulated as money and adornment across western North America.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Bamboo
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: A fast-growing grass used for building, slips, baskets, instruments and furniture.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Rattan
date_note: long-standing; export boom 19th c.
making_significance: Climbing-palm stems from Southeast Asian forests were split and woven into furniture and basketry.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Teak
date_note: long-standing; colonial forestry 19th c.
making_significance: A durable, oily hardwood used for dhows, houses and colonial ships, extracted with elephant labour in Burma.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Western red cedar
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: Northwest Coast peoples split planks, bent boxes, carved poles and wove bark from red cedar.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Ebony
date_note: Egyptian imports from Nubia and Punt; 17th-c. French ébénistes
making_significance: Dense black heartwood imported for Egyptian furniture and later veneered by Paris ébénistes.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Mahogany
date_note: major European demand from 1720s
making_significance: Caribbean and Central American mahogany, felled by enslaved woodcutters, became the prestige furniture wood of Georgian Britain.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Natural rubber
date_note: Mesoamerican rubber balls c.1600 BCE; Amazon and Congo booms 1879–1912; plantations in Southeast Asia from c.1900
making_significance: Latex from Castilla and Hevea trees, processed first in Mesoamerica, became a global industrial material extracted under coercion.
leaves_out: Congolese and Amazonian forced labour; Tamil plantation workers.
free_sources: Library of Congress (public-domain items); Wikimedia Commons

name: Gutta-percha
date_note: brought to European notice 1843; submarine telegraph cables from 1850s
making_significance: Malayan tree latex, mouldable when warm, insulated the first undersea telegraph cables and depleted forests.
object_types: cable insulation; golf balls; mourning jewellery
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Gourd
date_note: one of the earliest domesticated plants; long-standing
making_significance: Hard-shelled fruit used as vessels, instruments and floats and decorated by carving and pyrography.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Birch bark
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: Waterproof, flexible bark sewn into canoes and containers and used as a writing surface.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Palm leaf
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: Talipot and palmyra leaves were processed into manuscript folios and thatch.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; British Library (public-domain digitised items)

name: Papyrus
date_note: c.3000 BCE
making_significance: A Nile sedge made into writing sheets, boats, sandals and rope.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Paper
date_note: c.2nd c. BCE in China
making_significance: A felted sheet of plant fibre that carried writing, printing, wrapping, windows and money.
free_sources: National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data; Wikimedia Commons; Gallica BnF (public-domain items)

name: Lacquer sap
date_note: c.6000 BCE (Kuahuqiao)
making_significance: Sap of Toxicodendron and related trees, cured in humidity to a hard waterproof film.
leaves_out: Skin reactions for tappers and lacquerers.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Gum arabic
date_note: long-standing; major Atlantic trade from Senegal 17th–19th c.
making_significance: Acacia gum from the Sahel bound watercolours and inks and sized textiles; Europeans competed for the Senegal gum trade.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Bitumen
date_note: bitumen-coated reed boats c.5500 BCE (As-Sabiyah)
making_significance: Natural bitumen waterproofed boats, set inlays and held mosaics in Mesopotamia.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Sandalwood
date_note: long-standing in India; Pacific sandalwood trade c.1790s–1840s
making_significance: Fragrant wood carved into boxes and images; the Pacific sandalwood rush stripped Fiji and Hawaiʻi forests for the China market.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Frankincense and myrrh
date_note: approximate; Egyptian Punt expeditions; South Arabian trade
making_significance: Aromatic tree resins tapped in Dhofar and the Horn, burned in temples and used in embalming.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out)

name: Copal
date_note: long-standing; ongoing
making_significance: Tree resin burned as incense in Mesoamerican ritual and deposited as offerings.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Celluloid
date_note: Parkesine 1862; celluloid patented by the Hyatts 1870
making_significance: A semi-synthetic plastic that imitated ivory and tortoiseshell and made film stock.
free_sources: Google Patents / national patent offices (public documents); Wikimedia Commons

name: Bakelite
date_note: Leo Baekeland 1907
making_significance: The first fully synthetic plastic, moulded into radios, telephones and jewellery.
free_sources: Google Patents / national patent offices (public documents); Cooper Hewitt via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Commodity plastics
date_note: polyethylene 1933; mass consumer use after 1945
making_significance: Cheap petroleum-based polymers made disposable goods and packaging possible and now pollute oceans.
leaves_out: Waste and pollution borne by the Global South.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Cooper Hewitt via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked)

name: Plywood
date_note: patents from mid-19th c.; industrial boom 1900s–1940s
making_significance: Cross-laminated veneers make stable sheets, moulded by Aalto and the Eameses into furniture.
free_sources: MoMA collection (link out; metadata CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Tubular steel
date_note: Marcel Breuer's club chair 1925–26
making_significance: Bent seamless steel tube, borrowed from bicycles, became the material of modernist furniture.
free_sources: MoMA collection (link out; metadata CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Portland cement concrete
date_note: Joseph Aspdin patent 1824
making_significance: Hydraulic cement with aggregate became the most used building material in the world and a major carbon emitter.
free_sources: Google Patents / national patent offices (public documents); Wikimedia Commons

name: Reinforced concrete (material)
date_note: Monier 1867
making_significance: Steel-reinforced concrete enabled frames, shells and mass housing worldwide.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Glass curtain wall
date_note: Crystal Palace 1851 as precursor; Fagus Factory 1911; post-1950 spread (e.g. Lever House 1952)
making_significance: Non-structural glass walls hung on frames defined the corporate modern building.
materials_techniques: float glass; steel and aluminium framing
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Rayon
date_note: viscose patented 1892; Courtaulds production 1905
making_significance: Regenerated cellulose fibre imitated silk; carbon disulphide poisoned factory workers.
free_sources: Google Patents / national patent offices (public documents); Wikimedia Commons

name: Nylon
date_note: Wallace Carothers at DuPont 1935; stockings 1939
making_significance: The first fully synthetic textile fibre, used for stockings and wartime parachutes.
free_sources: Google Patents / national patent offices (public documents); Smithsonian Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Polyester
date_note: Whinfield and Dickson 1941
making_significance: A petroleum-based fibre now the most-produced textile fibre, central to fast fashion and microplastic pollution.
free_sources: Google Patents / national patent offices (public documents); Wikimedia Commons

name: Carbon fibre
date_note: high-strength fibres from late 1950s–1963
making_significance: Very strong, light carbon filaments in resin made aircraft parts, bicycles and prosthetics.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Silicon
date_note: silicon transistor 1954
making_significance: Purified silicon wafers carry the integrated circuits of digital devices.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries (US public domain)

name: Lithium
date_note: commercial lithium-ion battery 1991
making_significance: Lithium from Andean salt flats and Australian hard rock powers rechargeable batteries, raising water and Indigenous rights questions.
leaves_out: Atacameño and other Indigenous communities' water rights.
free_sources: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries (US public domain); Wikimedia Commons

name: Guano
date_note: Peruvian guano boom c.1840–1880
making_significance: Seabird droppings dug from Peruvian islands by indentured Chinese workers fertilised industrial agriculture.
free_sources: Library of Congress (public-domain items); Biodiversity Heritage Library (public domain); Wikimedia Commons

name: Coltan
date_note: tantalum demand for capacitors from 1990s
making_significance: Tantalum ore mined by hand in eastern DR Congo supplies electronics and has financed armed conflict.
free_sources: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries (US public domain); Wikimedia Commons

name: Cobalt
date_note: cobalt-blue glass in Egypt from the reign of Thutmose III (c. 1450 BCE), using Western Desert alum; cobalt blue on Abbasid ceramics 9th c.; DR Congo supplies most battery cobalt today
making_significance: Cobalt coloured blue-and-white ceramics for a millennium and now goes into batteries, much of it hand-dug in the DR Congo.
free_sources: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries (US public domain); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons
